description: We are interested in Moon Base
summary:
Analog Scout is a planetary analogue discovery and mission-planning platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It identifies places on Earth that resemble 11 selected Moon and Mars targets, including NASA's proposed Moon Base location, Artemis III candidate regions and Mars rover sites.

The platform combines a global search of 91,636 terrestrial land cells with 15-factor characterization of listed locations, interactive maps, live data probes and explainable site comparisons. Its unique features include Ask Why, which explains scientific similarities using transparent rules, and Analog within Reach, which identifies promising locations based on travel accessibility. Beyond discovery, users can build a 3D lunar or Martian base and simulate a 60-day mission.

By connecting scientific research, accessible analogue discovery and mission simulation, Analog Scout helps researchers better prepare for future human exploration beyond Earth.
details:
Q: What does it do or how does it work?

A:

Analog Scout identifies and compares terrestrial environments with real locations on the Moon and Mars. It has three main components:

  1. Discover: The Twin Finder compares 11 lunar and Martian targets with 30 characterized Earth sites. Global Search evaluates 91,636 Earth land cells at 0.5° resolution to identify new analogue candidates.
  2. Explain: Users can probe locations using live NASA and ESA data, compare environmental and geological characteristics, and use Ask Why to understand why two locations match and where specific experiments should be conducted.
  3. Simulate: Users can build a 3D lunar or Martian base and run a 60-day mission simulation to examine factors such as energy, resources, sunlight, radiation and crew survival.

The platform also generates downloadable scientific reports in Markdown and JSON formats.

Q: What benefits does it have?

A:

  • Broader discovery: Searches beyond traditionally recognized analogue locations to identify new potential research sites.
  • Scientific transparency: Explains similarity scores through individual factors, original data sources and clearly identified estimates.
  • Better research planning: Helps researchers identify suitable locations for testing drills, rovers, dust protection systems and life-detection instruments.
  • Improved accessibility: Analog within Reach identifies potentially useful analogue sites that are closer to a research team's starting location.
  • Mission preparation: The 3D base simulator allows users to explore operational challenges before establishing a real extraterrestrial habitat.

Q: What is the intended impact of the project?

A:

Our intended impact is to improve the preparation, planning and accessibility of future Moon and Mars exploration. By identifying and characterizing terrestrial analogue environments, we aim to help researchers conduct more targeted field studies and evaluate exploration technologies under relevant environmental conditions.

The platform also encourages wider participation in planetary research by helping student teams and research groups discover accessible analogue locations instead of relying exclusively on remote and expensive field destinations. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to better-informed exploration planning and the development of technologies for sustainable human presence beyond Earth.

Q: What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

A:

We developed Analog Scout as a web-based application using:

  • Programming languages: TypeScript and Python.
  • Frontend: React and Vite.
  • 3D visualization: Three.js.
  • Interactive mapping: MapLibre GL.
  • Data visualization: Recharts.
  • State management: Zustand.
  • Testing: Vitest and TypeScript type checking.
  • Development and deployment: Node.js, npm, Kiro, Claude and GitHub Pages.

Data integration: NASA POWER, MODIS, LRO, NASA GIBS, SWIM, THEMIS, Curiosity and Perseverance datasets, ESA Copernicus DEM, Mars Express, ExoMars, JAXA Kaguya, ISRO Chandrayaan-2, CNSA Tianwen-1 and Chang'e 4, and other open geological datasets.

Kiro and Claude assisted with development, drafting and presentation preparation. The application itself does not call an AI service; its explanations use deterministic, rule-based calculations.

The application is software-based and does not require dedicated physical hardware.

Q: How is your project creative?

A:

Our creativity comes from combining scientific discovery, explainability, accessibility and interactive simulation into one platform.

  • Global analogue discovery: Rather than only comparing established research locations, we screen 91,636 terrestrial land cells to identify previously under-explored candidates.
  • Explainable intelligence: Ask Why provides understandable answers to why a location is a match, why another location scores differently, and where a particular experiment should be conducted. Its explanations are generated using fixed rules rather than chatbot responses, allowing every score to be traced back to its underlying factors.
  • Analog within Reach: We introduce accessibility as part of analogue discovery by showing how much scientific similarity users can obtain within different travel distances.
  • Interactive planetary simulation: Users can construct a lunar or Martian base in 3D and simulate a 60-day mission, turning scientific findings into a more engaging engineering experience.

We also implemented automated validation, with 214 tests reported passing in our presentation, including checks that explanations correctly account for similarity scores.

Q: What factors did your team consider?

A:

We considered environmental, geological, scientific and practical factors when identifying and evaluating terrestrial analogues.

  • Environmental conditions: Temperature, extreme cold, dryness, temperature variation, ground ice, bare ground and wind conditions.
  • Geological characteristics: Rock types, volcanic activity, impact structures, slope, terrain roughness, water-laid materials and salt deposits.
  • Habitability: Availability of liquid water, environmental limitations on life, and conditions relevant to potential life-detection research.
  • Planetary conditions: Low-angle sunlight, polar illumination and similarities in environmental processes.
  • Accessibility: Distance from existing research locations and the travel requirements from a user's starting city.
  • Data reliability: Original measurement sources, estimated values, limitations of global datasets and the need for further live probing or field verification.

We also distinguish between locations that share similar environmental conditions and those that experience the same geological processes. This prevents a similarity score from being mistaken for proof that two locations are scientifically identical.
